newsitem.title: USA: Zinc market calm over looming LME backwardation.
newsitem.headline: Zinc market calm over looming LME backwardation.

text.p: Although the LME zinc cash to three months spread was poised to slide into backwardation for the first time in five years, traders said much of the stocks are in strong hands and were unlikely to be dumped if spread-based financing evaporated, traders said.
"I certainly think a backwardation will happen soon and I think it could last a good while," a broker for an LME ring dealer said.
Zinc was last in backwardation, or spot prices above forwards, in the third quarter of 1992.
Traders need a contango, or higher forward prices than cash, to pay storage costs for metal.
On Tuesday LME zinc prices rose to a fresh 6-3/4 year high with the cash to three months contango narrowing to $2/$3 a tonne.

"I think zinc is ready to explode," said industry analyst David Cook of Lake Engineering. "LME stocks are close to six weeks of supply and we are going to see further reductions, especially in the last four to five months of this year."
LME zinc stocks on Tuesday fell 950 tonnes to 423,100 tonnes.
But with good fundamentals in the U.S., and Europe also picking up, there may not be much surplus metal to offload into LME warehouses to exploit any backwardation, traders said.

U.S. zinc premiums have softened in recent weeks but appear to be holding at 4.50 to 4.75 cents a lb over LME cash. But premiums in Europe have risen some $20 to about $40 a tonne in warehouses in Rotterdam, dealers said.

"If you think the market will continue to rise, and most people who look at the fundamentals think this market will get tighter, I would not necessarily push a lot of zinc into warehouses," Ed Schmidt of producer Big River Zinc said.
Nevertheless, for physical merchants sitting on inventory, a prolonged backwardation would wipe out their ability to finance inventory, and could force them to dump metal.
"It's not going to be good," a broker said.
Brokers estimated that last year, zinc could have been financed forward to about December this year, therefore some metal will come onto the market over the next six months.

But the bulk of zinc stocks seen to be in the hands of one leading trade house in any case. "It doesn't matter if you can finance them or not if you are holding all the aces," an LME broker in New York said.
Meanwhile not everyone is convinced that zinc's latest surge is simply due to good fundamentals, but has also been prompted by a tussle between the longs and the shorts.
The gains have also been too rapid and the market needs a downside correction, some brokers said.
"I think it's more technically driven at the moment," a New York dealer said.
But China continues to cause nervousness.
The zinc market believes the country is short and saddled with some metal which is no longer LME-deliverable, and it will have to be re-refined.

In addition, a Chinese smelter has also sold forward some 60,000 tonnes of extra metal for export all at once. "Before they actually have it to deliver, they are going to have to roll it over into the first few months of the year, which is happening now," a broker said.
On Monday China's Zhuzhou smelter said Swiss trader Glencore had withdrawn a complaint made to LME about the quality of its TORCH brand.
Traders said the talk of complaints reflects the battle between major longs and shorts.
With a market in backwardation, it becomes more difficult for those who are short to roll their positions forward, Cook said. "It could cause some problems," Cook added.
((New York Commodity Desk 212-859-1646))
